description: We are an enthusiastic and focused team ready for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our team combines strong skills in technology, data, and creative design. We love space and science, and we work great together to solve hard problems. We are fully prepared, organized, and excited to build an awesome project for this hackathon!
summary:
We made Aegis Monitor, a web prototype for an autonomous smart spacesuit health‑monitoring system. Aegis Monitor shows live data from the spacesuit sensors -heart rate, blood oxygen SpO2 body temperature and stress levels - on a mission‑control dashboard. When Aegis Monitor sees a condition, like hypoxia or cardiac stress it immediately triggers an alert and starts life‑support actions: oxygen boost, limb compression and emergency auto‑injection.

Aegis Monitor solves the problem of watching crew health on deep‑space missions. On Mars the delay to Earth can be up to twenty minutes so remote medical help is not possible. Aegis Monitor moves from watching to actually intervening. The suit does not warn the astronaut, it acts.

We used open NASA Human Research Program data about stress responses, in microgravity. With that data we set Aegis Monitor’s alert thresholds to match physiological risks. Aegis Monitor shows how an intelligent suit can give crew members seconds and keep them alive when they are alone.
details:
Our project, Aegis Smart Suit, is an autonomous health-monitoring system designed for astronauts on deep-space missions. Unlike traditional spacesuits that only collect data, our suit actively intervenes when a crew member's life is in danger.

The suit is equipped with embedded biometric sensors that continuously monitor heart rate, blood oxygen levels, core temperature, and stress. A built-in AI analyzes this data in real time. If vital signs drop to critical levels - such as oxygen falling below 90% or a sudden spike in heart rate-the suit immediately activates life-support responses. It automatically boosts oxygen flow, tightens limb compression to maintain blood pressure, and can deliver an emergency auto-injection. Additionally, the suit uses thermochromic fabric that changes color to visually signal distress to other crew members, even if radio communication fails.

The need for this project is critical. During a mission to Mars, communication delays with Earth can reach up to 20 minutes. In a medical emergency, Ground Control cannot intervene in time. Our suit fills this gap by acting autonomously in the first few seconds, preventing hypoxia, loss of consciousness, and cardiac arrest.

To develop this concept, we used the NASA Human Research Roadmap data on cardiovascular adaptations in microgravity to calibrate our alert thresholds. For the visual concept of the suit, we used AI image generation tools (with visible watermarks, as required).

Our creativity lies in the shift from "passive monitoring" to "active life-support." The suit doesn't just warn the astronaut - it physically helps them survive. We considered the harsh realities of space: communication delays, isolation, and the limitations of the human body in microgravity.
